title: A Very Simple RSS Reader for Linux
excerpt: Here I am introducing the brand new simplest RSS reader for linux
content: Hello, Linux community! Introducing my simple RSS reader — built with proxy flexibility in mind. Hello, people! After moving to China, I started running into quite a few limitations when using Linux applications, largely due to the Great Firewall (GFW). It made me rethink how I handle network connections on my Linux desktop. I'm not particularly fond of using TUN mode or system-wide proxy settings on Linux. In my experience, they can sometimes be glitchy, and I don't like the idea of routing all my system traffic through a proxy when only certain applications actually need one. What I really wanted was something much simpler: the ability to configure a proxy directly within an application, so that only the traffic from that particular app goes through the proxy, leaving everything else on my system untouched. That became the primary motivation behind this little project. I started developing a simple RSS reader, with one main goal in mind: making proxy configuration as easy and straightforward as possible. No need to mess around with system-wide network settings or rely on TUN mode just to get an individual application working. Along the way, I realized that I also wanted more control over the reading experience. So I added support for custom fonts and font sizes, allowing users to personalize the interface and make reading more comfortable. And here we are! The first stable version, Simple RSS Reader v1.0 , is finally ready. I've been using and testing it for quite some time, and so far, I haven't run into any new bugs. Of course, there's always room for improvement, and I have plenty of ideas for additional features down the road. This is a relatively small project, but I built it to solve a problem I personally encountered, and I hope it might be useful to someone else facing similar frustrations. I'm happy to share it with the Linux community! If you're interested, give it a try. Feedback, suggestions, and bug reports are always welcome. They will help me make this little application better. Thanks for checking it out, and happy reading! ### Hello, Linux community! Introducing my simple RSS reader — built with proxy flexibility in mind. Hello, people! title: A Beginner’s Guide to Email Aliases: Protect Your Privacy Online
excerpt: Your Email Address Is More Exposed Than You Think
content: Why This Matters: A Recent Example In October 2026, the game company Capcom confirmed a data breach affecting its Capcom ID service. According to the company, 11,774,247 email addresses were leaked along with account details such as creation dates, login dates, and the IP address used at the last login. Most accounts didn’t have passwords stolen, but the leaked email addresses are still a problem. Capcom warned users to watch out for suspicious emails, since attackers can use leaked addresses to send convincing phishing messages that pretend to come from the company. source This shows a common risk. If you use one email address for everything, such as games, shopping, newsletters, and banking, then one leak connects all of those accounts to you. Anyone who gets that address can target you across all of them. An email alias is a simple way to reduce this risk. What Is an Email Alias? An email alias is a second email address that forwards messages to your real inbox. You can make a different alias for each website or service. If one alias gets leaked or starts receiving spam, you can turn it off or delete it, and your main address stays private. Think of it like giving out a different phone number for each store you shop at. Your real number stays hidden, and you can stop a single number without changing your whole phone line. Option 1: Apple Hide My Email (for iPhone and Mac users) If you use an iPhone or iCloud account, this is often the easiest option. Open Settings on your iPhone. Tap your name at the top. Tap iCloud . Tap Hide My Email . Tap Create New Address , give it a label (like “Shopping”), and tap Continue . Use the new address when signing up for a website or app. Messages sent to that address will arrive in your normal inbox. Option 2: Firefox Relay (works on any device) Firefox Relay is a free service from Mozilla, the company behind Firefox. Go to relay.firefox.com and sign in with a Firefox account (free to create). Click Create a mask (Mozilla’s name for an alias). Copy the new address. Use it when signing up for a service. Emails sent to it will be forwarded to your real inbox. You can disable or delete any mask at any time from the same page. Tips for Using Aliases Well Use a different alias for each service. Create one for games, one for shopping, and one for newsletters. Turn off aliases that get spam. If an alias receives unwanted mail, disable it. This is one of the main benefits of aliases. Keep your real address for important accounts. Use your main email for banking, taxes, and government services, where you need a reliable address. Still be careful with emails. Even with aliases, check the sender before clicking links, and go directly to a website instead of using links in unexpected emails. Save your aliases in a password manager. This helps you remember which alias went with which account. Quick Checklist Pick a method: Apple Hide My Email, or Firefox Relay. Create an alias for your next sign-up. Give each service its own alias when possible. Disable any alias that starts getting spam. Stay alert for phishing emails, especially after a known data breach. Using email aliases takes only a few minutes to set up, and it can limit the damage when a company like Capcom has a breach. Your real email address stays out of the spotlight, and you stay in control of who can reach you. ### Why This Matters: A Recent Example In October 2026, the game company Capcom confirmed a data breach affecting its Capcom ID service. According to the company, 11,774,247 email addresses were leaked along with account details such as creation dates, login dates, and the IP address used at the last login. Most accounts didn’t have passwords stolen, but the leaked email addresses are still a problem. Capcom warned users to watch out for suspicious emails, since attackers can use leaked addresses to send convincing phishing messages that pretend to come from the company. title: Why the GUI version of Clash is so glitchy?
excerpt: A frustrating experience with the Linux RPM build of Clash Verge Rev, and why I switched to a terminal-based alternative.
content: I recently tried a proxy client called Clash Verge Rev on Linux. It’s often described as one of the most popular Clash clients, and I’d been told the same thing when I asked ChatGPT and Claude for recommendations. Before version 2.5.8, everything worked fine. After I installed 2.5.8 from the RPM package, which is the installer format used by Fedora and Red Hat, things started falling apart. My connection kept cutting out in short bursts, and the problems got worse over time. At one point I couldn’t even watch a simple YouTube video in 1080p without it stuttering and buffering constantly. That was my limit. I wanted something that actually works well on Linux. Finding a Better Option While searching, I came across clash-for-linux . Unlike Clash Verge Rev, it’s a TUI (terminal user interface), meaning it runs in a text-based terminal window instead of a graphical app with buttons and menus. That might sound intimidating, but setup was just a few simple commands. Once it was running, I could set it to start automatically with my computer and mostly forget about it. The difference was immediate. The GUI version used more system resources, responded slowly, and kept glitching. The terminal version ran smoothly, responded quickly, and stayed out of my way for the rest of the day. If you’re having similar problems with a graphical proxy client on Linux, it may be worth trying a lightweight terminal option. Just be sure to read the setup instructions carefully, since they’re written for people comfortable with the command line. title: Markdown Editor Recommendation
excerpt: My experience trying several Markdown editors for blog writing, and the one I ended up choosing
content: I write my blog posts in Markdown, a simple plain-text format where symbols like # for headings and ** for bold show how the text should look. I wanted an editor that looks similar to Obsidian , a popular app for taking notes in Markdown. I started with Ghostwriter , a lightweight Markdown editor that was easy to install. On Fedora, a Linux distribution, I only needed to run sudo dnf install ghostwriter , and it was ready to use. Unfortunately, Ghostwriter had several serious display problems on Fedora 44, and they slowed down my writing. So I kept looking for a better option. Many people wonder why I didn’t simply use Obsidian. Obsidian is an excellent app, and I like it. It organizes everything into “vaults,” which are collections of notes that you can keep in one place. I have also installed a few community plugins to manage attachments and photos, and they work well for notes. However, the way Obsidian organizes vaults doesn’t match how I store my blog posts. What I need is a simple editor where I can open a Markdown file, write for the blog, and not worry about accidentally disrupting my blog’s folder structure. My search ended with MarkText . It is heavier than Ghostwriter, but it does two things I need very well: First, its live preview shows the formatted result as I type, so I can see headings, bold text, and links without switching windows. Second, once I add headings, it automatically builds a clickable outline on the left side of the screen. I can jump between sections of a long post with one click, which saves a lot of time. If you want a Markdown editor that is simple and focused on writing, rather than a full note-taking system like Obsidian, I highly recommend MarkText. title: Easy Terminal Proxy Switching on Linux: A Beginner’s Guide
excerpt: A guide for setup alias and bash function for easier proxy ON & OFF
content: Sometimes you want your terminal to send its internet traffic through a VPN or proxy, and sometimes you don’t. Typing long export commands every time gets tedious. This guide shows you how to add three short commands to your terminal: proxy_on turns the proxy on for the current terminal. proxy_off turns it off. proxy_status shows whether it’s on and where it’s pointing. Before You Start You need three things: A running proxy client. This guide uses Clash, which listens on a local “port” (a numbered doorway on your computer) of 7897. Open your Clash app and confirm it’s running. If you use a different client, or a different port, you’ll change the number in the steps below. A terminal. Any terminal app works. Basic comfort with a text editor. You’ll paste a block of text into a file called .bashrc, which is a settings file that runs every time you open a terminal. What’s a proxy? A proxy is a middleman. Your traffic goes to the proxy first, and the proxy forwards it to the internet. This can hide your location or route traffic through a VPN. When the proxy is off, your traffic goes straight out as usual. Step 1: Open Your .bashrc File In your terminal, type: nano ~/.bashrc nano is a simple text editor that runs in the terminal. The ~ symbol means your home folder, so ~/.bashrc is your personal settings file. Scroll to the bottom of the file using the arrow keys. Step 2: Paste the Proxy Functions Copy the block below and paste it at the bottom of the file: # --- Proxy Toggles for Clash Mixed Port --- proxy_on() { export http_proxy="http://127.0.0.1:7897" export https_proxy="http://127.0.0.1:7897" export HTTP_PROXY="http://127.0.0.1:7897" export HTTPS_PROXY="http://127.0.0.1:7897" export all_proxy="socks5h://127.0.0.1:7897" export ALL_PROXY="socks5h://127.0.0.1:7897" alias sudo='sudo -E ' echo -e "\e[1;32m[✔] Terminal proxy routing enabled (127.0.0.1:7897), sudo -E enabled\e[0m" } proxy_off() { unset http_proxy https_proxy HTTP_PROXY HTTPS_PROXY all_proxy ALL_PROXY unalias sudo 2>/dev/null echo -e "\e[1;31m[✘] Terminal proxy routing disabled. sudo -E disabled\e[0m" } proxy_status() { echo "Current Proxy Configuration:" echo "----------------------------" echo "http_proxy = $http_proxy" echo "https_proxy = $https_proxy" echo "all_proxy = $all_proxy" if alias sudo &>/dev/null; then echo "sudo alias = active (sudo -E)" else echo "sudo alias = inactive" fi } Save and exit nano : press Ctrl + O , then Enter to save, then Ctrl + X to exit. Tip: Only paste this block once. If you paste it twice, the functions get defined twice. Nothing breaks, but the file gets messy. Step 3: Load the New Commands Your terminal only reads .bashrc when it starts, so either open a new terminal window or run: source ~/.bashrc Step 4: Try It Out Turn the proxy on: proxy_on You should see a green message confirming the proxy is enabled. Check the status: proxy_status This prints the proxy addresses currently in use and whether the sudo shortcut is active. Turn the proxy off: proxy_off You should see a red message confirming it’s disabled. Step 5: Confirm It Really Works Commands like proxy_on only change your terminal, so the best test is to see whether your internet address changes. Run this while the proxy is on: curl https://ifconfig.me Then run proxy_off and try again. If the address differs between the two runs, the proxy is working. ( curl is a command-line tool for fetching web pages. It’s installed on most Linux systems. On Fedora, you can install it with sudo dnf install curl if needed.) How It Works, in Plain English Each function does a simple job: proxy_on sets several environment variables . These are named notes that programs read when they start. Many command-line tools, such as curl , wget , and git , check these notes and send their traffic through the proxy if they find one. The variables come in both lowercase and uppercase because different programs look for different versions. The socks5h lines use a different proxy protocol called SOCKS5. The h at the end means DNS lookups (converting website names into addresses) also go through the proxy, which avoids leaking which sites you visit. alias sudo='sudo -E ' creates a shortcut so that when you type sudo , it runs as sudo -E . The -E flag keeps your proxy settings when running commands as administrator. Without it, sudo usually wipes your environment, and proxy settings disappear. proxy_off removes all these variables and the sudo shortcut. The 2>/dev/null part hides any error message if the alias was never set. proxy_status prints the current values so you can see what’s active. Troubleshooting command not found: proxy_on You probably didn’t reload your settings. Open a new terminal or run source ~/.bashrc . Also check that you pasted the code into ~/.bashrc and not a different file. The proxy is on, but websites don’t load Your proxy client probably isn’t running, or it’s using a different port. title: A Complete Overhaul For My Personal Tech Blog!
excerpt: Here you are my first post! Announcement for my brand new personal tech blog come online!
content: Hello, everyone, and welcome, fellow netizens! I’m popping in to say hi. My personal website has been sitting on GitHub for about ten years without an update, so it’s time for a renovation. Today I’m launching my brand-new tech blog. It’s simple by design: I write posts in local Markdown files, convert them to HTML, and push them to a remote repository for online display. I did look at plenty of free blog templates on GitHub, but I didn’t need much beyond the basics. As a developer, I mostly use Markdown for code logs and notes, so what I really wanted was a blog that turns Markdown into HTML and serves it online. That’s it. With some help from AI, I built this template in a few hours and spent another hour or two testing it. And ta-da, it’s done! Consider this the official launch day announcement.
